traveler: Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
title: The Hero of Two Worlds: the Ship Bought Against the King, Six Prisons, and the Earth of Bunker Hill
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Château de Chavaniac, Auvergne: birth in the black towers
stops.campa: In a fortified manor of black volcanic stone, set among the Auvergne hills and long on lineage rather than cash, Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier is born. His father, Colonel Michel du Motier, is killed by a British cannonball at Minden two years later, and the estate with its debts passes to an infant. The boy grows up among peasants and a household of women, with no father to teach him a court he has never seen. He is two years old and the head of the house.
suggested_refs: The Château de Chavaniac in Haute-Loire, birthplace and lifelong property of the Motier family
sources: Laura Auricchio, The Marquis: Lafayette Reconsidered (2014)
Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: Hôtel de Noailles, Paris: the marriage
stops.campa: At sixteen he is married to Marie Adrienne Françoise de Noailles, fourteen and a half, in the chapel of her family's townhouse. Neither chose the other; the Duc d'Ayen arranged it two years earlier and kept the couple apart until the bride was older. The Noailles are among the first families of Versailles, and the match lifts an orphan out of a provincial manor into the inner ring of the French court. Adrienne will follow him into an Austrian prison twenty-one years from this room, and will not be asked to.
suggested_refs: The Hôtel de Noailles, rue Saint-Honoré, seat of the Noailles family in Paris

stops.name: Metz garrison: the Duke of Gloucester at table
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the anecdote is carried by nineteenth-century biographers and treated by modern historians as embellished
stops.campa: At a regimental dinner in the Metz garrison the Duke of Gloucester, brother to the King of England, speaks of the rebellion in the American colonies and of the men making it. Lafayette is seventeen, a lieutenant in the Noailles Dragoons, bored by garrison duty and by a court that finds him stiff and provincial. He says afterward that his heart was enlisted at that table. Nineteen months later he has bought a ship and is at sea against the king's orders.
suggested_refs: The site of the Governor's Palace at Metz, marked by a later statue of Lafayette

segments.name: The Ship Bought Against the King

stops.name: London: presented at the court he is about to fight
stops.campa: Weeks before crossing an ocean to fight the British army, Lafayette spends three weeks in London with the Prince de Poix, hosted by the Marquis de Noailles, French ambassador and his wife's uncle, and is presented to George III. He declines an invitation to see the naval works at Portsmouth, judging it dishonourable to inspect the defences of men who are entertaining him. Then he goes home, hides for a week, and goes to sea. The ministry he is deceiving is his own.
suggested_refs: The London embassy of the Marquis de Noailles, February 1777

stops.name: Pauillac, Gironde estuary: the Victoire drops downriver
stops.campa: The Victoire, a merchant ship Lafayette bought with borrowed money and loaded with muskets, drops down the Gironde toward the Atlantic. He is nineteen and has no leave to go. Royal orders for his arrest are already riding south, and his own father-in-law the Duc d'Ayen has asked for them. The ship will wait for him in a Spanish harbour while he doubles back overland, a fugitive from the government whose fleet will one day anchor for him in the Chesapeake.
suggested_refs: The Pauillac quay and its plaza marking the 1777 embarkation
sources: Stanley J. Idzerda, ed., Lafayette in the Age of the American Revolution, vol. 1

stops.name: Pasaia (Los Pasajes), Spain: the sailing
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict: Auricchio gives 20 April, Wikipedia 26 April; the earlier date is used here and the discrepancy is unresolved
stops.campa: At a Basque harbour hidden deep in its green inlet, Lafayette rejoins the Victoire and orders her to sea in defiance of the order recalling him. Two months of open Atlantic follow, unescorted, in a ship no navy would protect. He is seasick most of the way and spends the crossing learning English out of a dictionary and writing to a wife of seventeen whom he did not tell he was leaving. Adrienne is carrying their second child. A plaque on the quay still names the departure.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at Pasaia marking Lafayette's 1777 departure
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: North Island, Winyah Bay: wading ashore
stops.campa: The Victoire makes land in the marshes at the mouth of Winyah Bay, and Lafayette wades ashore below Georgetown into a country at war that has never heard of him. He sleeps his first American night in the house of Major Benjamin Huger. The family name will matter twenty years later, when Huger's son crosses Europe to break him out of an Austrian fortress. Nine hundred miles of Carolina and Virginia road lie between this beach and the Congress in Philadelphia.
suggested_refs: The Benjamin Huger plantation on North Island, Lafayette's first night on American soil
sources: Elizabeth Pinckney Huger, Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881)

stops.name: Independence Hall, Philadelphia: the unpaid major general
stops.campa: Congress, sick of French volunteers arriving with signed contracts for high rank, means to send this one home. Lafayette offers to serve at his own expense and without command, and on the last day of July Congress commissions him major general at nineteen. Five days later he meets George Washington at a Philadelphia dinner. Washington is forty-five and childless; Lafayette has been fatherless since he was two. Six weeks later he is shot through the leg at Brandywine.
suggested_refs: Journals of the Continental Congress, resolution of 31 July 1777

stops.name: Brandywine Creek, Chadds Ford: the shot through the calf
stops.campa: On the Brandywine the American right is turned and the line breaks. Lafayette gets off his horse and works the retreat on foot, reforming men who have stopped listening to anybody, and takes a musket ball through the calf. He stays on the field until Washington orders a surgeon to him. The wound is his credential: Congress and the army both stop reading him as a rich boy with a title, and Washington writes asking that he be given a division of his own.
suggested_refs: Washington's dispatches of September 1777 reporting Lafayette's wound

stops.name: Valley Forge: the winter of shoes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the encampment's opening; Lafayette winters through to May 1778
stops.campa: Lafayette winters with an army that is barefoot in snow. He buys shoes and blankets for his division out of his own pocket. The Conway intrigue offers him Washington's command and he turns it down. To Versailles he writes that money is not enough and that France must send ships and men. In the huts along the Schuylkill he becomes American in the only way that counts to the men around him, which is that he stayed the winter. In February France signs the alliance he has been begging for.
suggested_refs: The Valley Forge encampment huts and the Conway Cabal correspondence

stops.name: Monmouth Courthouse, New Jersey: the wing in the heat
stops.campa: Lafayette commands a wing in the largest battle of the northern war, fought in heat that kills men without a shot fired at them. Charles Lee is given the advance, orders a retreat nobody can explain, and meets Washington's fury in the middle of the field. Lafayette holds his ground until the line reforms behind him. Lee is court-martialled and finished; the young Frenchman's standing is settled for good. He is twenty, and has been a major general for eleven months.
suggested_refs: The court-martial record of Major General Charles Lee, 1778

stops.name: Newport, Rhode Island: the alliance nearly breaks
stops.date_confidence: attested to the window 22-30 August 1778; the Battle of Rhode Island itself is 29 August and Lafayette is absent from it
stops.campa: The first joint operation of the new alliance comes apart in a storm off Rhode Island. D'Estaing's damaged fleet withdraws to Boston, Sullivan's militia melts away, and American officers sign a protest against the French that Lafayette refuses to endorse. He rides to Boston to argue with the admiral, then rides back and reaches the field as the last shots of the battle are fired. He has saved the alliance and missed the action, and the army credits him with both.
suggested_refs: Idzerda, Lafayette Papers vol. 2, on the Rhode Island rupture and the Boston errand

stops.name: Boston Harbor: the Alliance sails for France
stops.campa: Lafayette sails for France aboard the frigate Alliance to press the court in person for a fleet and an army under a French flag rather than another loan. He goes with Congress's blessing and a gold-hilted sword voted him by that body. Behind him he leaves an army that has watched him spend a fortune on its boots. In Paris he will be put briefly under house arrest for the unlicensed departure of 1777, two years late, then made a colonel of dragoons.
suggested_refs: The presentation sword voted to Lafayette by the Continental Congress, 1779

stops.name: Hôtel de Noailles, Paris: a son named for Washington
stops.campa: A son is born and christened Georges Washington Louis Gilbert du Motier de La Fayette. The name is a foreign policy. Adrienne, who buried their first daughter in 1778 while her husband was in America, receives Marie-Antoinette in person in these rooms; the queen calls on her to mark the hero's return. Sixteen years later the boy will be shipped across the Atlantic and housed at Mount Vernon under Washington's own roof while both his parents are locked in an Austrian fortress.
suggested_refs: The baptismal record of Georges Washington de La Fayette, Paris, December 1779

stops.name: Boston: the Hermione makes landfall
stops.campa: The frigate Hermione lands Lafayette at Boston with the news the war has been waiting for: Rochambeau is coming, with six thousand men and a fleet behind them. Bells ring in the town. He rides for Washington's headquarters and hands over the confirmation that turns a colonial rebellion into a war between European powers fought on American ground. It is the answer to the letters he began writing at Valley Forge. He has been gone fifteen months and comes back with an army.
suggested_refs: The frigate Hermione, carrier of the Rochambeau dispatch, April 1780

stops.name: Richmond, Virginia: the boy who cannot be caught
stops.date_confidence: attested to the April-June 1781 campaign; day defaulted
stops.campa: Sent south with twelve hundred men to hold Virginia against Cornwallis and the turncoat Benedict Arnold, Lafayette refuses every offer of open battle. He marches, burns bridges, keeps a day's distance, and lets the British wear out the Tidewater roads behind him. To Washington he writes from the march. Cornwallis chases him up the Tidewater through the spring and catches nothing, and in the summer turns for the coast at Yorktown with Lafayette's men still behind him.
stops.quote: not strong enough even to get beaten
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to Washington, Virginia, spring 1781, in Idzerda, Lafayette in the Age of the American Revolution, vol. 4
suggested_refs: Lafayette's Virginia correspondence, April to June 1781

stops.name: Green Spring, Virginia: the baited trap
stops.campa: Cornwallis baits a trap near the Jamestown ford, showing a rear guard where his whole army is waiting. Anthony Wayne's advance walks into it. Lafayette, riding forward to look at the ground himself, sees the deception minutes before it closes and pulls out what he can. Two guns are abandoned when their horses are shot. About a hundred and forty Americans are lost and his own horse is killed under him. It is the sharpest reverse of his war. Cornwallis marches on to Yorktown regardless.
suggested_refs: Cornwallis's report to Clinton on the Green Spring action, July 1781

stops.name: Yorktown, Virginia: Redoubt No. 10
stops.campa: Lafayette's light infantry division draws the assault on Redoubt No. 10, the smaller of the two works still holding the British left. He gives the order; Alexander Hamilton leads the column in with muskets unloaded and bayonets fixed, and the redoubt falls in about ten minutes. Four hundred French troops of the Royal Deux-Ponts take Redoubt No. 9 on the same night. The siege lines close, and Cornwallis has no wall left between his army and the guns.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Redoubts 9 and 10 on the Yorktown battlefield

stops.name: Yorktown, Virginia: the surrender
stops.campa: The British army marches out between the French and American lines and grounds its arms. Lafayette is twenty-four. He has pinned Cornwallis against the York River for a summer and stands now at the end of the war he crossed an ocean to join uninvited. Francisco de Miranda has spent that same summer raising silver in the counting-houses of Havana to pay the fleet that sealed the bay. Neither man has heard of the other. The silver and the siege lines are one operation.
suggested_refs: The Yorktown surrender field, 19 October 1781

stops.name: Cádiz: humanity has gained her cause
stops.date_confidence: attested by the letter's own dateline, Cadiz, 1 January 1783
stops.campa: Lafayette is at Cadiz with a Franco-Spanish expedition fitting out against the British West Indies when word arrives that the preliminaries of peace are signed and the invasion is off. He writes to a cousin in France with the news, in a sentence that will be misquoted for two centuries afterward. He is twenty-five, a general in two armies, and the war that made him is finished. Six years remain before his own country asks him to do the whole thing again at home.
stops.quote: My grand affair appears settled, for America is certain of her independence, humanity has gained her cause, and liberty will never be without a place of refuge.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to his cousin, Cadiz, 1 January 1783, in Memoirs, Correspondence and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, vol. II, p.48
suggested_refs: Memoirs, Correspondence and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, vol. II, p.48
sources: Memoirs, Correspondence and Manuscripts of General Lafayette (Saunders and Otley, 1837), vol. II

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the Estates-General and a draft of rights
stops.date_confidence: attested; the draft Declaration is presented 11 July 1789
stops.campa: The Estates-General meets for the first time since 1614, and Lafayette takes his seat among the deputies of the nobility, elected by men who mostly disagree with him. In July he lays before the National Assembly a draft Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, written with Thomas Jefferson's help in Paris. The American document is twelve years old and was drafted three thousand miles from the king it renounced. This one is drafted down the corridor from Louis XVI.
suggested_refs: Lafayette's draft Declaration of the Rights of Man, 11 July 1789, with Jefferson's marginal corrections
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: The Bastille and the Hôtel de Ville, Paris: the tricolor
stops.date_confidence: attested; the National Guard command is conferred 15 July
stops.campa: The fortress falls to the crowd, and the next day the electors of Paris acclaim Lafayette commander of the new National Guard. He gives it a cockade of blue and white and red: the colours of the city wrapped around the colour of the Bourbons. The flag France still flies is assembled in a week by a man who means to save the monarchy. In Murcia a boy of eleven called José de San Martín is a year from the cadet rolls; Manuel Belgrano is at Salamanca; Francisco de Miranda has been in London three weeks.
suggested_refs: The site of the Bastille and the Paris municipal records of July 1789

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the October days
stops.campa: Thousands of Parisian women march on Versailles for bread, and the National Guard follows because it will not be left behind. Lafayette arrives near midnight, gets an hour of sleep, and wakes to a palace already breached. He brings Marie-Antoinette out onto the balcony, bows, and kisses her hand in front of the crowd. The gesture buys the royal family the road to Paris instead of the pikes. It also fixes him in every popular print as the man who guards the queen.
suggested_refs: Contemporary accounts of the Women's March on Versailles, collected in Schama, Citizens
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: Mount Vernon: the key crosses the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1790 by Lafayette's covering letter; day defaulted
stops.campa: The main key of the Bastille crosses the ocean as a gift from Lafayette to George Washington, carried by Thomas Paine and delivered to the President. It is a son's tribute and a claim at once: that the two revolutions are one revolution, and that Washington is the father of both. Washington hangs it in the hall at Mount Vernon, where it still hangs. Lafayette's own son will be living under that roof five years from now, while his father is in a cell.
stops.quote: I would never have drawn my sword in the cause of America, if I could have conceived that thereby I was founding a land of slavery.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette in conversation at Paris, recalled from memory by Thomas Clarkson in a letter to Mrs. H. G. Chapman, Playford Hall, 3 October 1845, printed in The Liberty Bell (Boston, 1846), p.64; not a Lafayette letter
suggested_refs: The Bastille key in the central passage at Mount Vernon
sources: Lafayette to Washington, March 1790, Idzerda, Lafayette Papers vol. 5

stops.name: Champ de Mars, Paris: the Fête de la Fédération
stops.campa: On the first anniversary of the Bastille's fall, before some hundreds of thousands on the Champ de Mars, Lafayette climbs the altar of the fatherland and administers the civic oath, and Louis XVI swears to uphold the constitution. It rains all day and nobody leaves. This is the high water of the constitutional monarchy: a king who has sworn to the constitution, and a general who believes he can hold him to it. In the same month José de San Martín is entered on the cadet rolls of the Regiment of Murcia.
suggested_refs: The official proceedings of the Fête de la Fédération, 14 July 1790
sources: Official Fête de la Fédération proceedings, 1790

stops.name: Champ de Mars, Paris: the volley
stops.campa: On the same ground, one year later, a crowd gathers to sign a petition demanding the king's removal after his flight to Varennes. Martial law is declared, the red flag goes up, stones are thrown, and the National Guard fires. Dozens die on the field where the oath was sworn. Lafayette is present and in command. The Paris crowd never forgives him and the Jacobin clubs have their proof. He has fired on the only constituency that would have accepted the constitutional monarchy he wanted.
suggested_refs: The National Assembly inquiry into the Champ de Mars firing, 1791

stops.name: Metz: the Army of the Centre
stops.date_confidence: attested; note the appointment precedes the declaration of war on Austria of 20 April 1792 by four months
stops.campa: Lafayette takes command of the Army of the Centre at Metz, in the garrison town where a duke's dinner conversation once turned him toward America. France declares war on Austria four months later. In June he writes to the Legislative Assembly denouncing the Jacobin clubs by name, then leaves his army without leave and repeats it to their faces from the bar of the house. He is shouted down. Within seven weeks he is a fugitive from the revolution whose guard he commanded.
suggested_refs: Lafayette's letter of 16 June 1792 to the Legislative Assembly against the Jacobin clubs
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: Tuileries Palace, Paris: the tenth of August
stops.campa: The palace is stormed and the Swiss Guard killed to a man; the monarchy ends in an afternoon. With it ends the constitution Lafayette swore to on the Champ de Mars, and the whole project of a French revolution with a king inside it. The Assembly declares him a traitor. Napoleon Bonaparte, a captain on half pay, watches the crowd take these courtyards. He will hold them himself as emperor within twelve years. Lafayette, who commanded the guard that used to hold this gate, is out of France in nine days.
suggested_refs: The Tuileries courtyard, 10 August 1792

stops.name: Frontier near Rochefort, Austrian Netherlands: the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the village of capture is given differently across memoirs and Austrian military correspondence
stops.campa: Lafayette rides out of France with a small staff, meaning to pass through Austrian territory to neutral ground and then to America. Austrian troops take him in the border woods. He is not treated as a prisoner of war: the coalition has caught the man who commanded the National Guard, drafted the Declaration, and sent the Bastille's key to a republic, and it intends to keep him out of the world entirely. The accounts differ on the village. They agree on the woods.
suggested_refs: Austrian military correspondence on the arrest of Lafayette, August 1792
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier de La Fayette'

stops.name: Wesel fortress, Prussia: solitary
stops.campa: Prussia holds him first, in the fortress at Wesel on the Rhine, in solitary confinement, without books, letters, or news of France. Officially he does not exist: the coalition will not call him a prisoner of war, because that would concede he is the soldier of a state. His wife and children are in France under the Law of Suspects, and the property is sequestrated. For two years neither he nor Adrienne is permitted to learn whether the other is alive.
stops.quote: It is well known that the regimen of my five years' imprisonment was not favourable to literary occupations.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette, 'To the Reader', Memoirs, Correspondence and Manuscripts of General Lafayette, vol. 1 (1837), written long after the captivity
suggested_refs: Prussian prison registers cited in Gottschalk, Lafayette Between the American and the French Revolution
sources: Louis Gottschalk, Lafayette Between the American and the French Revolution

stops.name: Magdeburg fortress: the casemate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1793; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Moved deeper into Prussia, Lafayette spends a year in a casemate cell under the ramparts at Magdeburg, below ground level, damp, nearly lightless. His health breaks here in ways that never mend afterward. Francisco de Miranda watched Frederick the Great's army manoeuvre on this same ground in 1785, a free traveller carrying letters of introduction. Nine years separate the free traveller from the prisoner on the same ground. Prussia then hands its prisoner to Austria.
suggested_refs: The casemates of the Magdeburg citadel
sources: Gottschalk, Lafayette Between the American and the French Revolution

stops.name: Olmütz (Olomouc) fortress, Moravia: the number in the register
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1794; French Wikipedia's section heading 'Olomouc (1795-1797)' refers to the final phase only and is not the arrival date
stops.campa: Austria takes delivery and shuts him in the fortress at Olmütz in Moravia, entered on the rolls under a number rather than a name and forbidden to write or receive a letter. He will be here three years. Sixty years on, the same citadel holds Mikhail Bakunin, condemned to death twice and chained to a wall before Austria hands him over to Russia. Bakunin wants the state abolished and Lafayette wanted it written down. Austria puts them in the same casemates.
stops.quote: ...the few lines the mother ventured to write to her son, and which she sent to the American Consul, were stopped in Vienna and returned.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to Colonel Francis K. Huger, 1797, in Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881), p.45, on the Olmütz censorship; 'the mother' is Adrienne and 'her son' is Georges Washington de Lafayette in America
suggested_refs: The fortress prison of Olomouc, Moravia
sources: French Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier de La Fayette'

stops.name: Olmütz: Bollmann and Huger
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 November 1794; some accounts give 8 November
stops.campa: A German physician, Justus Erich Bollmann, and a young South Carolinian named Francis Kinloch Huger mount a rescue. They intercept Lafayette on his supervised carriage exercise outside the walls, fight the guards, and get him onto a horse. He rides the wrong way, is retaken within a day, and both rescuers go to prison themselves. Huger is the son of the man in whose house Lafayette slept his first night in America. The failure buys six months of harsher confinement.
stops.quote: How hardly they have treated you, my admirable friend! I fear that your sufferings during your captivity may have injured your health.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to Colonel Francis K. Huger, written from Hamburg in 1797, in Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881), p.45
suggested_refs: Elizabeth Pinckney Huger, Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881)
sources: Huger, Statement of the Attempted Rescue (1881)

stops.name: Olmütz: Adrienne comes in
stops.date_confidence: traditional; October 1795 is the widely cited arrival and Lafayette's own letter says twelve months after the escape attempt, but no primary dateline was reached in this pass
stops.campa: Released from a Paris prison after Thermidor, and armed with an audience granted by the Emperor at the Hofburg in Vienna, Adrienne obtains not her husband's freedom but permission to share his cell. She arrives at Olmütz with their daughters Anastasie and Virginie, and the doors are locked behind all three. She never asks to leave. Her health fails there and never recovers. She has already lost her grandmother, her mother, and her sister to the guillotine in a single July afternoon.
stops.quote: You knew that twelve months later my wife and daughters shared my captivity.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to Colonel Francis K. Huger, written from Hamburg after his release, in Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881), p.45
suggested_refs: Notice sur Madame de Lafayette, published posthumously by her daughters
sources: Huger, Statement of the Attempted Rescue (1881)

segments.name: La Grange and the Last Revolution

stops.name: Olmütz: the nineteenth of September
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Treaty of Campo Formio is signed 17 October 1797, a month after the release, so the release cannot be a term of that treaty
stops.campa: Bonaparte, dictating to Austria from northern Italy, makes the prisoner's release a personal condition of his negotiation, and after five years the doors open. Lafayette walks out with a wife who can barely stand. He is forty, stateless, and owns nothing. The Directory in Paris will not have him back, and the American republic he helped to make cannot receive a man his own country calls a traitor. He has been out of the world since the summer the monarchy fell.
stops.quote: It was on the 19th September, five months after hostilities had ended, that we were liberated.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to Colonel Francis K. Huger, in Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881), pp.45-46
suggested_refs: The Leoben preliminaries and Bonaparte's correspondence on the Olmütz prisoners, 1797
sources: Huger, Statement of the Attempted Rescue (1881)
Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: Hamburg: handed to the American consul
stops.campa: Brought overland across Germany, Lafayette is handed to the American consul at Hamburg, the one official on the continent willing to take responsibility for him. He writes at once to Huger, the young man who tried to break him out and went to prison for it. Two more years of exile follow in Holstein and Holland before Bonaparte's amnesty lets him set foot in France. He will never hold a command again. Five years have taken his health, his fortune, and his party, and left his opinions.
stops.quote: The same friend whose liberties you so generously undertook and whose beating heart turns to you in the moment he regains his life and liberty, here addresses you, and hastens to offer you the tribute of his inexpressible and unbounded gratitude.
stops.quote_source: Lafayette to Colonel Francis K. Huger, Hamburg, undated, in Statement of the Attempted Rescue of General Lafayette from Olmutz (1881), p.44
suggested_refs: The American consulate at Hamburg, October 1797
sources: Huger, Statement of the Attempted Rescue (1881)

stops.name: Château de La Grange-Bléneau, Courpalay: the moated farm
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1800-1834; the year of settlement is approximate and the day is defaulted
stops.campa: Lafayette settles at a moated château in Brie, inherited through Adrienne's family, and farms it with American methods, merino sheep, and imported seed. He refuses Napoleon's senate, refuses the Legion of Honour, and is one of a handful who vote against the life consulate. Visitors arrive from both revolutions. Alexander von Humboldt dines with Jefferson in Washington in 1804. Lafayette holds no office at all for eighteen years, and the merino flock is the whole of his public life.
suggested_refs: The Château de La Grange-Bléneau at Courpalay, Seine-et-Marne, and its Lafayette archive
sources: Lasteyrie, Vie de Madame de Lafayette

stops.name: Castle Garden, New York: the return after forty years
stops.date_confidence: attested; he reaches Staten Island on 15 August and lands at Castle Garden on 16 August
stops.campa: Lafayette lands on the Battery to the largest civic welcome the continent has given any living person, invited by President James Monroe, whose wife once walked into a Paris prison to signal that the United States was watching and probably saved Adrienne's life. He is sixty-six and the last surviving major general of the Revolution. Over some thirteen months he will visit all twenty-four states, and towns and counties will take his name in a wave that has never quite stopped.
suggested_refs: Levasseur, Lafayette in America, the secretary's day-by-day record of the tour
sources: Wikipedia, 'Visit of the Marquis de Lafayette to the United States'

stops.name: Mount Vernon: at the tomb
stops.campa: Lafayette comes to Mount Vernon and goes down into the vault where Washington lies. He is left alone with the coffin and comes out weeping, carrying a ring holding a lock of the general's hair. His son Georges Washington de Lafayette, who lived in this house as a boy while both his parents were shut in Olmütz, walks the grounds beside him. The key of the Bastille still hangs in the passage where Washington hung it thirty-four years ago. He will come back to this vault once more before he sails home for the last time.
suggested_refs: The old tomb at Mount Vernon, visited 17 October 1824
sources: Wikipedia, 'Visit of the Marquis de Lafayette to the United States'

stops.name: Bunker Hill, Charlestown: the cornerstone
stops.campa: Fifty years to the day after the battle, Lafayette lays the cornerstone of the Bunker Hill Monument while Daniel Webster speaks and survivors of the fight sit in front of the platform. He has soil from the hill packed up and shipped to France. He intends to be buried under it, and he tells the crowd so. He is arranging his own grave in public and in the wrong country. He was seventeen and in a French garrison on the day these men held this hill. Nine years remain to him.
suggested_refs: Daniel Webster's Bunker Hill Monument oration, 17 June 1825

stops.name: Paris: the July days
stops.campa: Three days of barricades put the Bourbons out for good, and the crowd wants Lafayette. At seventy-two he takes the National Guard again, and a delegation offers him the presidency of a republic, which in plain speech means a dictatorship. He refuses it. He brings Louis-Philippe onto the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville wrapped in a tricolor and embraces him in front of the crowd, and calls what follows the best of republics. He spends his last four years regretting the phrase.
suggested_refs: The balcony of the Hôtel de Ville, 31 July 1830
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette'

stops.name: Rue d'Anjou-Saint-Honoré, Paris: the death
stops.campa: Lafayette dies at his Paris house at seventy-six, of an illness taken standing bareheaded in February rain at another man's funeral. Adrienne has been dead twenty-six years. He has outlived Washington, the Bourbons, Napoleon, and every general who served beside him in America. The government of Louis-Philippe, nervous of the crowd, orders a military funeral guarded so heavily that the public cannot get near the coffin and the eulogies are not delivered.
suggested_refs: Funeral notices and press accounts, Paris, May 1834

stops.name: Cimetière de Picpus, Paris: the American ground
stops.campa: He is buried at Picpus, in the private cemetery grown up around the pits into which the guillotine of the Place du Trône-Renversé emptied, among them Adrienne's grandmother, her mother, and her sister, all three killed on one afternoon in July 1794. He lies beside Adrienne under the earth carried home from Bunker Hill; his son scatters it over the coffin. The Marquis de Lafayette is buried in American ground, in Paris, a few steps from the pit that took his wife's family.
suggested_refs: The Picpus enclosure, the Terror pits, and the Lafayette grave

stops.name: Lafayette Square, Washington: the standing bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1891; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: A standing bronze of Lafayette by Alexandre Falguière and Antonin Mercié is set at a corner of the square opposite the President's house, one of four monuments to foreign officers of the Revolution placed at the four corners. Rochambeau, Kosciuszko, and von Steuben take the others; Andrew Jackson rides the middle of the square on his horse. The square had carried Lafayette's name for sixty-seven years before anyone put his figure in it. Across the street, presidents work with a Frenchman's statue in the window.
suggested_refs: The Falguière and Mercié monument, Lafayette Square, dedicated 1891

stops.name: Cimetière de Picpus, Paris: four words at the grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the ceremony; the attribution of the words is contested between Colonel Stanton and General Pershing and no source consulted resolves it
stops.campa: Three months after the United States enters the war, an American column marches to the Picpus cemetery on the Fourth of July and a colonel named Charles E. Stanton speaks four words at the grave. Popular memory hands them to Pershing, who was standing beside him and did not say them. One hundred and forty years after Lafayette waded ashore in Carolina, an American army is in France. The Daughters of the American Revolution keep a flag over the stone and renew it each Independence Day.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Colonel Charles E. Stanton at Lafayette's grave, Picpus Cemetery, 4 July 1917; the attribution is contested between Stanton and Pershing
suggested_refs: The DAR flag over the Lafayette grave and the annual Fourth of July ceremony at Picpus
